Lowland vs. Upland Conditions: Appropriate forest species differ depending on lowland
or upland planting locations, although the differences in elevation in low-lying Robson
County are small. Pine species require adequate drainage, so they are better suited for
slightly more upland areas. They also have better ﬁnancial returns, so they are preferred
when possible. Bottomland hardwoods are more suited for wetter, lowland areas, although
some hardwoods will grow in most locations in the county. The FEMA 100-year and
500-year ﬂoodplains were used to approximate the locations of lowland areas. This criterion
was not exclusionary in identifying opportunity areas but was used as an additional layer
of information to enhance understanding of existing conditions and tree species suitability.
The FEMA 100-year and 500-year ﬂoodplain layers were merged and intersected with the
opportunity areas to identify lowland areas that would be more suitable for bottomland
hardwood forest species. Other sites that could support forests well on slightly higher
ground were designated as pine areas.

claims.quote:
environment in river basins, composed of multiple environmental factors
that characterized the erosion risks and erosion rate, which is a measure
of the exposure of the land to the environment by some risk (natural loss
of soil). To calculate the natural vulnerability (secondary data), the process-
ing, classiﬁcation and integration of environmental factors (primary data)
were carried out in a GIS environment. Each factor represents a vulnerabil-
ity agent and corresponds to a raster layer (information plan).
The basic territorial units are the elementary cells of information on en-
vironmental factors and anthropogenic factors. Each cell (pixel) contains
the set of information to perform the functions in the development of the
geographical unit of the hydrographic basin. The primary data of each
cell (considered as one pixel per unit from remote sensing raster image)
was composed of environmental factors: geology (geological units), pedol-
ogy (soil type), relief (slope) and anthropogenic factors (context of land-
scape and suitability for AFS):
2.2.2.1. Geology. The geological data raster was obtained from the Geolog-
ical Map of the State of São Paulo. The raster ﬁle was clipped from the edge
of the study area and classiﬁed according to Table 2 for the thematic map
production and its use in Eq. (1). Area information (ha) of each geological
class was also extracted.
2.2.2.2. Soil type. The information on soil types in the study area were ex-
tracted from the Soil Map of the State of São Paulo. The raster ﬁle was ex-
tracted, projected and classiﬁed at category level: Order and reclassify
according to MDCA propositions and ranking (Table 2). A cross-
tabulation was also performed to obtain the area according to class.
2.2.2.3. Slope. The slope data were derived from the Digital Elevation Model
(DEM) reprocessed by the Brazilian National Institute for Space Research
(INPE) with a spatial resolution of 30 m × 30 m, from the scanned informa-
tion of the orbital sensors from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission
(SRTM), which represents the terrestrial topography with a spatial resolu-
tion of 90 m × 90 m. The DEM model has been utilized to generate the
slope map. Though the Spatial Analyst tools, was performed ﬁlls sinks in
the surface raster to remove small imperfections in the data, and then
slope was calculated by the bilinear resampling method (default) of the
Surface and Slope functions of ArcMap. The elevation output of slope values
is expressed in percentage and was classiﬁed in a range according to
the classiﬁcation proposed by Embrapa (2006): 0–3% (ﬂat); 3–8% (gentle
undulating); 8–20% (Undulating); 20–45% (high undulating); 45–75%
(mountainous) and 75–100% (cliff). Subsequently, the layer was reclassi-
ﬁed according to the weights of the MDCA classiﬁcation for the processing
of natural vulnerability.
The algebraic operations were carried out with the same methodology
performed in the tools, operators and functions of the ArcGIS Spatial Ana-
lyst extension to perform the geographical analysis of the secondary data
set. Through information plan algebra, equated by the arithmetic mean of
all factors and by the hierarchy of processes analysis (Analytic Hierarchy
Process-AHP), the weight (that is, AHP normalized classiﬁcation) of the
various classes for each environmental and anthropic factor was classiﬁed
in terms of the relative strength of each class within each factor and the im-
portance of these for the analysis, based on the review of the relevant liter-
ature for each factor and in the decision making of the relative importance
among the criteria calculated using the pair comparison matrix proposed by
Saaty (1987, 1977), Table 2.

MethodsX 10 (2023) 102052 
The section Method validation provides an overview of the source and processing of the selected criteria (geodataset factors) used 
in this methodology. All data sets are georeferenced and are either vector (shapeﬁle) or raster ﬁles so that the overall processing 
of the geodatabases follows the speciﬁc executions of each GIS package. Therefore, the methodology description will emphasize the 
general procedures and tools for the creation, conversion, and analysis of each input database (EF and AF) and the combination of 
the information sets for the corresponding outputs (V, ES, SIPA-AFS). 
Step 1: natural vulnerability (V) 
The determination of V is the ﬁrst step in the development of this method and is based on the evaluation framework of the Land 
vulnerability (Vu) methodology proposed by Pissarra [16] . With this, we establish a general basis that reinforces the priority of the 
areas of highest risk of natural land loss in the agroecosystem, regardless of which decision-making approach may be employed. The 
method of identiﬁes the fragility of the natural environment in watersheds based on multiple environmental factors that characterize 
erosion risks, which is a measure of the exposure of land to the environment for some risk (natural soil loss). It is a multi-criteria 
spatial analysis implemented in GIS software, where land vulnerability (secondary data) is derived from the spatial distribution of 
three environmental factors: geology (G), soil (S), slope (SL), and, an anthropogenic factor: land cover - primary data. Each factor 
represents an agent of vulnerability and corresponds to the input of a layer (raster) in the spatial modeling of map algebra. The factors 
are expressed in numerical (SL) and categorical (G, S) scales, but independently are evaluated within the landscape and subsequently 
converted to a shared dimensionless scale (rank and weight) to allow consistent aggregation and mutual comparison within the 
mathematical framework of multicriteria decision analysis and thus estimate the natural vulnerability of the landscape. The MDCA 
method adopted was the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), which equates and weights each criterion (factor) by the arithmetic mean 
of the information plan and its relative importance among the criteria calculated by the pairwise comparison matrix as proposed by 
Saaty [58–60] , which evaluates the relative importance in a set of weights from 1 to 9. The participatory decision-making process 
consulted researchers specialized in forest conservation and sustainable production. The authors technical background and their 
articulation with diﬀerent stakeholders - small land owners and governance agents, were also considered [9] . The factors are ranked 
as to relevance in the landscape structure and as to the classiﬁcation of the attributes of each factor: geology (lithological types), 
soil (soil types), slope (slope classes), and land cover (land use and land cover classes). Additionally, all factors are ranked by their 
overall inﬂuence on natural vulnerability, as a dimensionless parameter to become comparable. The weight value is the importance 
of each factor on the landscape scale, higher weights point to the most important parameters, and higher rankings also indicate the 
most vulnerable classes. The consistency of judgments regarding the importance of factors to land vulnerability presented by Pissarra 
[16] is validated by the Consistency Index (CI) at a rate above < 0.1 [60] . All class ratings of each factor, factor ranking of importance, 
and weight are available in the supplementary material (sheet 1). Once the weights of each class and each factor are validated, the 
algebraic operations of the “Spatial Analyst Tool: Map Algebra/Raster Calculator ” functions of the ArcMap GIS combine the maps 
(raster ﬁles) corresponding to each factor and multiply them by the corresponding MDCA weights to determine the land vulnerability 
’according to the equation: 
𝑉 𝑢 = ( 0 . 056 𝐺 ) + ( 0 . 122 𝑆 ) + ( 0 . 263 𝑆𝑙 ) + ( 0 . 558 𝐿𝑈𝐿𝐶 ) 
(1) 
Where: Vu = land vulnerability; G = geology; S = soil; Sl = slope; LULC = land cover 
Here it is highlighted that in Pissarra [16] the default anthropogenic factor is land cover, and for this reason, the proposed indicator 
methodology (SIPA-AFS) assumes at ﬁrst as natural vulnerability (V) only the algebraic combination of environmental factors (G, S, 
Sl), i.e., it suppresses the aggregation of the LULC component, a partial application of Eq. (1) proposed in the previous methodology. 
Then, the map algebra for determining the natural vulnerability of the landscape only computes V = (0.056 G) + (0.122 S) + (0.263 
Sl). From the partial application of Eq. (1) a map of continuous values is generated depending mainly on the quantity and ratings of 
the classes of each factor. It is emphasized that the weighting of the weights of each class and the global importance of the factors was 
established in relation to the intrinsic potential for erosion, either by comparison of one factor in relation to the other, or intra-classes. 
In this methodology, we maintained the greatest weight for the slope factor, which has a direct expression in the intensity of water 
ﬂows and the kinetic potential of surface runoﬀ[ 61 , 62 ]. Following in importance the type of soil of the landscape by observing the 
erodibility coeﬃcient (K factor) of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE), reviewed in the literature [ 26 , 63 ]. Geology follows in 
expressiveness as an erosive agent but provides the basic conditions for inﬁltration of surface water ﬂows or mass movement [64] . The 
anthropogenic factor, to be used in step 2, holds the greatest weight in the decision making, as it reﬂects the actual exposure and risk 
of degradation and the socioeconomic and environmental demands for the implementation of the AFS. When drawing a vulnerability 
map this range is simpliﬁed through the equal interval classiﬁcation method, that divides attribute values into four equal size ranges 
where the highest values correspond to the highest risk of landscape degradation through soil erosion, sorted into 4 qualitative 
vulnerability classes: (1) Low vulnerability; (2) Average vulnerability; (3) High vulnerability; (4) Extreme vulnerability. In general, 
geoprocessing software provides many standard classiﬁcation methods that are used for classifying numerical ﬁelds for graduated 
symbology. In this case, in ArcMap we generate the 4 intervals from the classiﬁcation of the raster ﬁle, by the commands: Layer 
Properties/ Symbology/ Classiﬁed/Classify. We deﬁned only four classes to optimize the visualization in decision-making process 
and selected the equal interval classiﬁcation method to create classes of equal sizes, since the range of values is normally distributed. 
Step 2: exploratory scenarios (ES) 
This module is responsible for the aggregation of the anthropogenic factor to the evaluation of V, discriminated here in four 
anthropogenic factors (LU, FF, PLUC, PA), which represent the human pressure on the environment and its implications for the 
recovery of the landscape by the AFS. These are supporting indicators for the simulation of scenarios favorable to the implementation
